Bronisław Malinowski. The Polish-born British anthropologist who revolutionized ethnographic method through years of intensive participant observation in the Trobriand Islands.

Malinowski spent four years, from 1915 to 1918, in the Trobriand Islands conducting participant observation during World War I. This was extraordinary for its time. He documented kinship, exchange systems, magic, and daily life in unprecedented detail, establishing a completely new standard for what ethnographic fieldwork could achieve.

He championed functionalism — the idea that cultural practices and beliefs serve to meet psychological and social needs. This shaped how anthropologists explain rituals, taboos, and institutions. His approach emphasized learning the language, living among the people, and abandoning external judgment — what he called ethnographic realism.

In 1922, he published Argonauts of the Western Pacific, a monograph that presented ethnographic data with reflexivity about method. This established the standard for ethnographic monographs that is still followed today. His study of the kula ring, a ceremonial exchange system in the Trobriand Islands, became a foundational example of how economic systems embed cultural and social meanings.

Malinowski founded the London School of Economics' anthropology program, training a generation of British anthropologists including Evans-Pritchard and Radcliffe-Brown. He was a rival theorist to Radcliffe-Brown; the two debated functionalism versus structuralism, yet both proved foundational to British anthropology. Though they advocated different functionalism models, both helped define the discipline.
